item.title: Margaret Sullivan grades midterm coverage
item.description: Rosen recommends Margaret Sullivan's assessment of midterm press coverage, noting that she explicitly uses the frame of stakes rather than odds.

item.title: Exposure and accountability as different political tasks
item.description: Rosen connects his earlier thread about distinctions in media criticism with Brian Beutler's argument that exposure is not accountability.

item.title: An emergency setting for Trump coverage
item.description: Rosen revisits his March 2020 PressThink essay written in the voice of a newsroom editor explaining a different approach to Trump coverage.

item.title: Ellison, Trump, and access for CNN
item.description: Rosen highlights David Ellison's stated support for restoring CNN's access to cover Trump and argues that this conflict should lead coverage of the new CNN.

item.title: Not the odds but the stakes in election coverage
item.description: Rosen restates his proposed organizing principle for election coverage: Focus on consequences for American democracy rather than winning probabilities. He refers back to September 11, 2023.

item.title: David Ellison's claims about truth, trust, and Trump
item.description: Rosen highlights Status's questions at David Ellison's press conference and the tension between Ellison's appeal to truth and trust and his account of Trump's enthusiasm.

item.title: A revised recommendation of Polarization Is Not the Problem
item.description: Rosen again recommends Lilliana Mason's argument about polarization and both-sides journalism and invites readers' reactions.

item.title: The Daily Beast's character-driven election coverage
item.description: Rosen argues that the Daily Beast's character-driven approach offers an alternative to the view from nowhere, while making Trump its central character also brings costs.

item.title: An older PressThink post in a discussion of political advertising
item.description: Replying in a discussion of television stations' obligations around Trump-related advertising, Rosen offers a November 2004 PressThink post while acknowledging that it does not answer the precise question.

item.title: A reporter's account of Trump's lying
item.description: Rosen recommends a Canadian reporter's CNN account of studying Trump's rhetoric, public reactions to his lying, and the way it is covered.

item.title: Why the press pool fights matter
item.description: Rosen recommends a Washington Post column, shared by Brian Stelter, as an explanation of why disputes over press pool access matter.

item.title: Send the interns and the press pool boycott
item.description: Quoting On the Media's question about why journalists took so long to reconsider their norms, Rosen points to his January 2017 PressThink essay Send the interns.

item.title: A press pool without shared presidential video
item.description: Rosen shares Brian Stelter's account of a presidential appearance without a television camera supplying footage to the wider press corps.

item.title: Revisiting Send the interns
item.description: Rosen recommends his PressThink essay Send the interns, published on the second day of the first Trump White House.

item.title: The propaganda risks of a media merger
item.description: Rosen shares an argument that combining entertainment and news in a large propaganda structure could make it especially effective.

item.title: Which newsrooms make up the national mainstream press?
item.description: Rosen revisits his 2016 PressThink essay on party asymmetry and notes that its definition of the national mainstream press would differ today.

item.title: Margaret Sullivan on midterm stakes
item.description: Rosen shares Margaret Sullivan's plan to track midterm coverage with greater attention to consequences and less attention to winning probabilities.

item.title: Brian Williams on normalization in news coverage
item.description: Rosen shares a video in which Brian Williams responds to a question about extremism reaching public life. Rosen highlights Williams's observation about normalization.

item.title: A reader's comparison with George Lakoff
item.description: A reader compares Rosen's approach to election stakes with George Lakoff's moral framing. Rosen replies that he has not met Lakoff but sees similarities in their approaches.

item.title: Two weeks of reading for a journalism course
item.description: Rosen proposes beginning a journalism course with Tom Rosenstiel and The Elements of Journalism, followed by The Next Journalism: How the Press Must Change to Serve Democracy.

item.title: Election coverage: The stakes beyond the polls
item.description: Rosen points to Mike Podhorzer's midterm overview as an example of election coverage organized around consequences rather than winning probabilities.

item.title: Citizens Agenda '26: Help CDN pin down candidates on issues that matter to you
item.description: Jon Bauer explains how Cascadia Daily News is using the Citizens Agenda model for a fifth election season in Whatcom and Skagit counties. Readers submit and rank questions that reporters will put to candidates, shifting coverage toward voter priorities, engagement, and solutions rather than campaign horse-race narratives.

item.title: For Jay Rosen, American Press Needs to Become More Pro-Democracy
item.description: Interview with Jay Rosen for NYU's Journal of Political Inquiry, conducted by Pau Torres Pages. Rosen argues this is the worst time for American journalism because it is the worst time for American democracy, and presses his case that the American press must become more explicitly pro-democracy -- distilled in his slogan "not the odds but the stakes." He diagnoses the collapse of the Washington Post under Jeff Bezos, proposes a Washington Post Foundation/trust to insulate it from owners, assesses the defunding of public media and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, and questions Bari Weiss's ideologically driven leadership of CBS. He closes that the powerful will always find ways to be informed; the open question is whether publics, in the plural, will remain so.
